attribution_note: Ribhu to Nidagha: correct (chapter 5 opens with the speaker label 'Ribhu'). Whether Ribhu is Nidagha's teacher or father is read differently (Ayyangar/Brahmayogin: father); 'teacher' is safe in practice but don't assert kinship.
translation_note: Accurate. Warrier reads it slightly differently: spontaneous indifference to experiences that do not come of their own accord and hearty acceptance of those that do. Ayyangar glosses the pandita as a jivanmukta.
context: Chapter 5 continues Ribhu's teaching: the seven stages of ignorance and of knowledge, the danger of vasanas (latent tendencies), three kinds of 'I'-sense, and how a wise person lives among worldly affairs. Follows the rule 'let go of what is lost, take up what comes' (5.170). Ribhu now names the mark of the wise; next he says a person of gnosis, free of desire and aversion, is no more stained than a lotus leaf by water.
core_teaching: The wise naturally stop pining for future pleasures and fully enjoy what has already come.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Absence of longing for pleasures not yet attained, with natural enjoyment of what comes unsought, is the innate quality of the pandita, the jivanmukta who has perceived the supreme Self.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: The mark of a discriminating person is spontaneous indifference to experiences that do not come of themselves and hearty acceptance of those that do.

practical_reading: Enjoy today's meal, today's company, today's small win, without the background hum of 'and next...'.
misreadings: Not a ban on planning or hope
'Unforced' means this should not be a grim effort of suppression
not_for: someone whose present is painful (illness, grief), if told to 'enjoy what has come'

verified_ref: Maha Upanishad (Mahopanishad) 5.185-186, confirmed against the Sanskrit text on Sanskrit Wikisource, which carries its own verse numbers; Ayyangar's and Warrier's Adyar translations group verses in consistent blocks. These are the last two verses of chapter 5.
attribution_note: Ribhu to Nidagha: correct (chapter 5 opens with the speaker label 'Ribhu'). Whether Ribhu is Nidagha's teacher or father is read differently (Ayyangar/Brahmayogin: father); 'teacher' is safe in practice but don't assert kinship.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Removed by work' (kriyaya) = by action or effort (Ayyangar: through labour; Warrier: through effort). 'Vipra' (O Brahmin) is addressed to Nidagha.
context: Chapter 5 continues Ribhu's teaching: the seven stages of ignorance and of knowledge, the danger of vasanas (latent tendencies), three kinds of 'I'-sense, and how a wise person lives among worldly affairs. Ribhu has explained how ideation (sankalpa) sprouts from pure awareness and grows into misery, and urged Nidagha to uproot each idea with care, cutting ideas by ideas and the mind by the mind (5.178-184). He closes the chapter with this image of husk and tarnish, and the call to be industrious.

key_terms.sense: is removed by action or effort
one should be industrious, make effort

core_teaching: Our flaws may be natural, like husk on rice or tarnish on copper, but effort removes them; so keep working on yourself.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: As paddy husk and copper's tarnish come off only by labour, so does the impurity of the individual self. Though innate, it need not stay; it is surely removable, so put forth effort.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: As paddy husk or the black coating on copper is destroyed by effort, so may a person's mental impurities be. Like the grain's, the self's innate impurity can be destroyed; there is no doubt, so strive.

practical_reading: Don't despair of a habit or trait just because it feels like 'who I am'. Patient polishing works on copper and on people.
misreadings: 'Impurity' is not a statement that the person is bad or dirty
cautions: Words like 'impurity' or 'stain' can trigger shame; use 'rough edges' or 'tarnish' language in readings
not_for: someone struggling with shame or self-loathing, if 'impurity' is stressed

verified_ref: Maha Upanishad (Mahopanishad) 6.64-65, confirmed against the Sanskrit text on Sanskrit Wikisource, which carries its own verse numbers; Ayyangar's and Warrier's Adyar translations group verses in consistent blocks.
attribution_note: Ribhu to Nidagha (chapter 6 continues his teaching): consistent with the text, though no speaker label appears at these verses.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Doing the work that comes' (prapta-karma-kara): Ayyangar adds 'as they occur, in accord with previous karma'. 'Knowing the intent of others' hearts' (ashayajna): Ayyangar, able to read others' thoughts at a glance; Warrier, conversant with the thoughts of all beings.
context: Chapter 6 describes the person liberated while living (jivanmukta). Just before, Ribhu says one who rests in the state beyond all, filled with pure awareness, is neither agitated nor elated and does not sink in worldly life (6.63). These verses give the outward marks; next he urges Nidagha to roam the world as such a person, free of fever, seeming to engage but inwardly untouched.

key_terms.sense: doing the work that comes to hand
wanted and unwanted, likes and dislikes
one who understands others' inner intent

core_teaching: A free person does the work at hand, treats friend and foe alike, speaks kindly and perceptively, and so moves through the world without sinking.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Fulfilling daily tasks as they occur, seeing friend and foe alike, free of attachment and aversion, the sage neither grieves nor longs; speaking agreeably when asked and reading others' thoughts at a glance, he does not drown in worldly existence.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: One who does what falls to his lot, sees foe and friend alike, and is free of likes and dislikes is neither sad nor hopeful; who says what pleases all and speaks pleasantly when asked never suffers in this life.

practical_reading: A good day's template: do the task in front of you, be fair to people you like and dislike, speak gently, and try to understand what others really mean.
misreadings: 'Saying what is agreeable to all' is not people-pleasing or dishonesty
'Seeing friend and foe alike' does not mean ignoring real danger
not_for: someone facing an abuser, if 'see foe as friend' is applied
